To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) B cells from SLE patients secrete immunoglobulins spontaneously when cultured in the absence of any exogenous stimuli, and (2) the maturation of these cells to become immunoglobulin-secreting cells is not dependent on interleukin-2, interleukins 4 or 6.
B cells from SLE patients secrete high levels of immunoglobin spontaneously, and this is due to an intrinsic defect of these cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of B lymphocyte function in patients with systemic lup erythematosus and other rheumatic diseases.
the mechanisms involved in the regulation of B cell activation and immunoglobulin production.
the mechanisms of B cell activation and the role of B lymphocytes in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematous.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SLE B cells are already primed for immunoglobulin synthesis in vivo and that this priming process is independent of cytokines.
SLE B lymphocyte maturation and immunoglobulin synthesis are cytokine‐independent.
SLE B lymphocyte immunoglobulin production is already initiated and progresses in the absence of exogenous cytokine stimulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
B cells from SLE patients are already primed to produce immunoglobulins in the absence of exogenous cytokines.
the SLE B cells are already activated and mature in vivo and are able to produce immunoglobulin spontaneously.
B‐lymphocytes from patients with SLE are already committed to Ig‐synthesis, which can proceed independently of further stimulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SLE B lymphocyte immunoglobulin synthesis is independent of exogenous cytokine stimulation.
the SLE B lymphocyte has an intrinsic propensity to mature and secrete immunoglobulins.
SLE B lymphocyte immunoglobulin synthesis in vivo is not dependent on interleukins.
